primary_cause: Defensive healthcare got sold along with market after White House grim COVID projections of 100K-240K U.S. deaths. No clear UnitedHealth-specific announcement on March 29-31
secondary_factors: Rising uncertainty around insurer cost exposure from testing and treatment and policy response
store_description: This looks more like a macro de-risking move than a UNH idiosyncratic event. On April 1 Reuters said investors were dumping even defensive equities after the White House projected 100K-240K deaths which fits a modest UNH decline better than a company-specific shock.

primary_cause: Travel and mobility demand collapse tied to lockdowns. Uber had already told investors on March 18 it would hold analyst call on COVID-19 business impact. Rides later confirmed down 80% globally in April
secondary_factors: High-beta growth stock selling. Concern that Eats strength would not offset Rides weakness
store_description: UBER 9.0% drop was probably the market repricing a company whose core business depended on urban mobility right as the White House turned sharply more pessimistic on the pandemic. The stock was extremely exposed to worsening lockdown expectations and already-signaled COVID business stress.

primary_cause: Semiconductor and industrial demand fears as macro outlook deteriorated. No discrete Texas Instruments announcement on March 29-31
secondary_factors: TXN analog exposure to autos and industrials both hit hard by shutdown expectations
store_description: This looks like a cyclical semiconductor selloff rather than a TXN-specific event. On April 1 the market sold off broadly on worsening COVID expectations and for TXN that would have been amplified by its heavy exposure to industrial and auto end markets.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters reported on March 31 that U.S. March auto sales had fallen off a cliff because of coronavirus disruption. Tesla directly exposed to shutdown of Fremont factory idle from March 24 under stay-at-home orders
secondary_factors: High-beta unwind and uncertainty ahead of Q1 delivery data
store_description: TSLA 8.1% drop was not just market down. Reuters said U.S. March vehicle sales cratered and Tesla simultaneously faced a forced Fremont shutdown beginning March 24 creating a direct hit to both demand and production.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Simon had temporarily closed all U.S. retail properties on March 18 with closure supposed to run through March 29. By April 1 investors staring at likelihood malls would not quickly reopen. Mall-closure and rent-collection fears
secondary_factors: Real-estate and retail traffic panic as national COVID outlook worsened
store_description: SPG 14.3% fall had one of the clearest stock-specific stories: its entire domestic mall portfolio had already been shut and the end-of-March temporary deadline looked increasingly unrealistic as the White House warned of a brutal next phase. Investors were effectively pricing in a much longer traffic and rent freeze.

primary_cause: Utilities sold off with broader market despite being defensive. No clear Southern Company-specific March 29-31 headline
secondary_factors: General recession fears and concern around commercial and industrial power demand
store_description: SO 7.4% move is larger than you would expect from pure defensiveness but no distinct company event found in the 3-day window. Best read is broad equity liquidation day with utilities getting dragged down as investors sold almost everything after the White House death-toll warning.

primary_cause: Continued repricing of North American store closures and traffic collapse. Reuters reported on March 20 that Starbucks would close most company-operated cafes in U.S. and Canada for two weeks limiting service to drive-throughs
secondary_factors: Worsening U.S. COVID outlook and broader consumer-discretionary selloff
store_description: Starbucks 4.7% drop was likely an extension of the market reassessment of a company whose in-person traffic model had just been disrupted at scale. Reuters had already documented broad North American cafe closures and April 1 darker public-health outlook reinforced fears that the disruption would last longer than initially hoped.

primary_cause: Aerospace demand fears tied to air-travel shutdown. No Raytheon Technologies-specific Mar 29-31 Reuters item. Aerospace complex under pressure from collapsing air travel and supply-chain stress
secondary_factors: Merger and integration uncertainty and defense-adjacent industrial selling
store_description: RTX 3.1% drop looks mainly like aerospace contagion from the commercial aviation collapse rather than a fresh single-company headline. As travel demand fell apart and Boeing liquidity concerns stayed front of mind suppliers and adjacent names like RTX were repriced lower.

primary_cause: Semiconductor risk-off and broad tech selling. No discrete NVIDIA announcement in March 29-31 window
secondary_factors: Concern that fast-forming recession would hurt gaming enterprise and channel demand
store_description: NVDA 7.8% move appears mostly macro and sector-driven. On April 1 investors were aggressively dumping growth and cyclicals and semis were especially vulnerable because the pandemic threatened both end demand and supply-chain visibility.

primary_cause: Global store-closure and consumer-spending fears. Nike had already reported on March 24 managing through shutdowns while shifting inventory toward digital. Store closures remained obvious operating issue
secondary_factors: General discretionary selloff and recession fears
store_description: NKE 4.2% drop was likely investors extending the implications of widespread retail closures into a deeper recession scenario. Nike own late-March commentary already centered on disrupted physical retail and a pivot to digital and the April 1 market tone made that problem look longer and larger.

primary_cause: Broad semiconductor selloff. No Intel-specific March 29-31 announcement
secondary_factors: Concern that enterprise and consumer demand would weaken despite work-from-home tailwinds
store_description: INTC 4.1% decline looks more like sector beta plus recession fear than company news. The White House much grimmer April 1 COVID forecast increased expectations of deeper economic contraction which weighed on chipmakers even without a new Intel headline.

primary_cause: Semiconductor capital-equipment derating on recession fears. No Applied Materials-specific Mar 29-31 announcement
secondary_factors: Concern that customers would defer fab spending if downturn deepened
store_description: AMAT 5.5% fall was probably a leveraged version of the semiconductor risk-off trade. Investors were increasingly worried that if the pandemic worsened materially chip customers could slow equipment orders making capital-equipment names more vulnerable than defensive tech.

primary_cause: Industrial and aerospace demand fears. Honeywell later withdrew 2020 outlook on weak aerospace demand. Commercial-aerospace pressure already visible by late March. No separate Mar 29-31 HON release
secondary_factors: Broad cyclical selling and supply-chain uncertainty
store_description: HON 3.0% decline fits a company with meaningful exposure to aerospace and industrial end markets right as investors braced for a much deeper shutdown-driven recession. No clean Honeywell headline in the exact 3-day window so this is mostly cyclical macro repricing.

primary_cause: Anticipated credit losses and recession-driven bank de-rating. No Citi-specific Mar 29-31 release. Bank stocks under pressure from looming credit losses and recession expectations. Citi published same-day April 1 coronavirus impact outlook
secondary_factors: Near-zero rates line-draw and liquidity fears and broad risk-asset liquidation
store_description: C 8.6% drop looks like a classic early-pandemic bank move: investors were bracing for large reserve builds lower rates and a fast-deteriorating economy. The most plausible explanation is a sector-wide bank repricing amplified by Citi economic sensitivity.

primary_cause: Conglomerate exposure to rapidly worsening recession especially travel and cyclical holdings. No Berkshire-specific Mar 29-31 announcement. Meaningful exposure to economically sensitive businesses including insurance industrial transportation and airline holdings
secondary_factors: General financial-sector and market weakness
store_description: BRK-B 3.8% decline was likely a portfolio-look-through reaction rather than a single Berkshire headline. Investors were discounting the damage that a deeper COVID shock could inflict on Berkshire broad set of cyclical businesses and public-equity holdings.

primary_cause: Asset-manager earnings and AUM pressure from violent market declines. Reuters later reported BlackRock first-quarter AUM hit by market turmoil with net income falling to $806M from $1.05B year earlier. That mechanism already hitting stock on April 1
secondary_factors: Broad financial-sector selling
store_description: BLK 6.9% drop makes sense as investors priced the effect of Q1 market chaos on fee-linked assets under management. The business model was directly exposed to market-value declines and risk-off client behavior even without a fresh Mar 29-31 company release.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters reported on April 1 that Booking Holdings CEO Glenn Fogel tested positive for coronavirus. More importantly Booking was one of clearest public-travel exposures in market already pricing near-freeze in global bookings
secondary_factors: CEO positive-test headline and market-wide risk-off
store_description: BKNG 5.5% drop fits the view that online travel would be among the hardest-hit business models as lockdowns deepened. The direct headline on April 1 was that CEO Glenn Fogel had tested positive but the larger driver was still the near-shutdown of global travel demand.

primary_cause: Bank-sector repricing for recession reserve builds and lower rates. No Bank of America-specific Mar 29-31 announcement
secondary_factors: Liquidity and credit-draw concerns and broad market liquidation
store_description: BAC 6.9% decline looks like a straightforward pandemic bank selloff. Investors were increasingly focused on the scale of coming loan losses and the earnings hit from near-zero rates and April 1 grim White House guidance made that scenario look worse.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters had already reported Boeing was seeking $60B lifeline for aerospace industry after first reporting Boeing itself wanted tens of billions in government support. Liquidity narrative still hanging over stock into April 1
secondary_factors: 737 MAX overhang and broader aerospace panic
store_description: BA 12.4% drop had a much stronger single-name explanation than most stocks here. Boeing was still associated with an extraordinary request for public and private liquidity support while commercial aviation demand was imploding so April 1 darker COVID outlook worsened an already severe solvency and funding narrative.

primary_cause: Global industrial and recession fears. No Caterpillar-specific Mar 29-31 announcement
secondary_factors: Exposure to construction mining and energy customers facing shutdowns and spending cuts
store_description: CAT 4.0% move looks consistent with a cyclical industrial name being repriced for a steeper global downturn. On April 1 the market was reacting to a much more severe public-health and economic scenario and CAT end markets made it a natural casualty even without a fresh company headline.
